title: Mastering CI/CD with GitHub Actions: A Developer's Guide
summary:
Introduction: The CI/CD Imperative

In today's fast-paced software development landscape, Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Deployment (CD) are no longer optional luxuries but fundamental necessities. They empower development teams to deliver code changes more frequently and reliably, significantly accelerating the software development lifecycle. At its core, CI/CD is about automating the build, test, and deployment processes, allowing developers to focus on writing great code rather than getting bogged down in manual, error-prone tasks. This article will guide you through setting up a robust CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions, a powerful and flexible automation platform integrated directly into GitHub.

Why GitHub Actions?

GitHub Actions provides a seamless way to automate your workflows, from building and testing code to deploying applications. Its event-driven nature means that actions can be triggered by a wide range of GitHub events, such as pushing code, creating pull requests, or even scheduling tasks. The platform offers a rich marketplace of pre-built actions, allowing you to integrate with various services and tools without reinventing the wheel. This level of integration and extensibility makes it an ideal choice for modern development teams looking to streamline their operations. For businesses seeking to understand market dynamics, evaluating the success of such development practices can sometimes be compared to understanding the landscape of industries like real estate. For instance, understanding the factors that make Top Real Estate Companies in Delhi NCR successful involves analyzing their operational efficiency and market responsiveness, much like how CI/CD impacts software delivery.

Setting Up Your First CI/CD Pipeline

Let's walk through creating a basic CI/CD pipeline for a simple Node.js application. This pipeline will automatically build and test your code whenever changes are pushed to the repository.

1. Create a Workflow File

Navigate to your GitHub repository and create a directory named .github/workflows in the root of your project. Inside this directory, create a YAML file, for example, ci.yml.

2. Define the Workflow

Here's a sample ci.yml file:

name: CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Use Node.js 18.x
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18.x'
      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: npm ci
      - name: Run Tests
        run: npm test

Explanation:

  • name: The name of your workflow.
  • on: Defines the events that trigger the workflow (push and pull request to the main branch).
  • jobs: Contains one or more jobs that will run.
  • build-and-test: The ID of our job.
  • runs-on: Specifies the runner environment (Ubuntu latest).
  • steps: A sequence of tasks to execute.
    • actions/checkout@v3: Checks out your repository code.
    • actions/setup-node@v3: Sets up the Node.js environment.
    • npm ci and npm test: Commands to install dependencies and run tests.

3. Adding Deployment (CD)

To add deployment, you would extend this workflow. For example, you could add a deploy job that runs after build-and-test completes successfully. This might involve using actions to deploy to cloud providers like AWS, Azure, or Vercel.

# ... (previous steps)

  deploy:
    needs: build-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' # Only deploy from main branch
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to Production
        run: echo "Deploying to production..."
        # Add your actual deployment script here

Conclusion

GitHub Actions offers a powerful, integrated solution for implementing CI/CD pipelines. By automating your build, test, and deployment processes, you can significantly improve development velocity and code quality. The flexibility and extensive marketplace of actions allow for customization to fit almost any project's needs. Embracing CI/CD with tools like GitHub Actions is a critical step towards modern, efficient software development.

title: Unlocking Cloud Native: A Deep Dive into Kubernetes & Microservices
summary:
Introduction: The Microservices Revolution

The software development landscape has undergone a seismic shift. Gone are the days of monolithic applications, slowly being replaced by the agility and scalability offered by microservices. This architectural style breaks down complex applications into smaller, independent services, each responsible for a specific business capability. This approach fosters faster development cycles, improved fault isolation, and the ability to scale individual components. However, managing a distributed system of this nature presents unique challenges.

Orchestrating Complexity: The Role of Kubernetes

This is where Kubernetes (K8s) emerges as a game-changer. As the de facto standard for container orchestration, Kubernetes automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It provides a robust framework for handling the intricacies of microservices, abstracting away much of the underlying infrastructure complexity.

Core Kubernetes Concepts for Microservices:

  • Pods: The smallest deployable units in Kubernetes, typically encapsulating one or more containers that share resources. For microservices, a pod often runs a single service container.
  • Deployments: Manage the lifecycle of Pods, enabling declarative updates and rollbacks. This is crucial for zero-downtime deployments of microservices.
  • Services: Provide a stable network endpoint for a set of Pods, abstracting away the dynamic nature of Pod IPs. This allows other services to discover and communicate with your microservices reliably.
  • Ingress: Manages external access to services within the cluster, often handling HTTP and HTTPS routing, SSL termination, and name-based virtual hosting. Essential for exposing your microservices to the outside world.
  • ConfigMaps & Secrets: Allow for the decoupling of configuration data and sensitive information from container images, promoting better security and manageability.

Building Resilient Microservices with K8s

Kubernetes inherently provides several features that contribute to building resilient microservices. Its self-healing capabilities automatically restart failed containers, reschedule pods on healthy nodes, and replace terminated pods. Health checks (liveness and readiness probes) ensure that traffic is only sent to healthy instances of your services. Furthermore, Kubernetes' declarative nature means you define the desired state, and the system works to maintain it, providing a strong foundation for distributed systems. This is particularly important when considering complex deployments, much like navigating the diverse offerings from Top Real Estate Companies in Delhi NCR requires careful planning and execution.

Beyond the Basics: Advanced Patterns

As your microservices architecture matures, you'll encounter more advanced patterns that Kubernetes can help implement:

  • Service Mesh (e.g., Istio, Linkerd): Provides advanced traffic management, observability, and security features at the platform level, independent of application code.
  • CI/CD Pipelines: Integrating Kubernetes with CI/CD tools (like Jenkins, GitLab CI, Argo CD) automates the build, test, and deployment process for your microservices.
  • Observability: Leveraging tools like Prometheus for metrics, Grafana for visualization, and Elasticsearch/Fluentd/Kibana (EFK) for logging is critical for understanding the behavior of your distributed system.

Conclusion: Embracing the Cloud Native Future

Kubernetes has become indispensable for organizations adopting microservices. By understanding and leveraging its core concepts and advanced features, developers can build, deploy, and manage scalable, resilient, and observable microservice-based applications. The journey into cloud-native development is ongoing, but with Kubernetes as a powerful ally, the path to modern, agile software delivery is clearer than ever.

title: Snapshotting a DigitalOcean Droplet while it's running
summary:
DigitalOcean lets you snapshot a Droplet while it's running, and its docs are careful about it. They say a live snapshot "may result in performance degradation and compromise data consistency", and that many databases only guarantee a consistent disk if you stop them or power the Droplet off first. That's sensible advice. I wanted to know what it means in practice: what a snapshot of a busy Droplet contains when you restore it, whether the Droplet slows down while it's taken, and what powering off first actually costs you.

The setup

One Droplet in Frankfurt, the 2 GB / 1 vCPU size with a 50 GB disk, running Ubuntu 24.04 and Postgres 16 with its default settings. On it, two writers ran the whole time:

  • Postgres. One numbered row per transaction, about 100 a second. Every insert logged when it was sent and how long the commit took.
  • Files. The same fixed-width numbered line, about 100 a second, appended to two files. One file got an fsync after every line. The other was only written, so its lines sat in the page cache until Linux decided to flush them.

Then I took snapshots through the API, timed them by polling the action, restored each one to a new Droplet and looked at what was on the disk. Each restored copy was destroyed as soon as I had checked it, and each snapshot deleted.

I did six live snapshots: three with about 2.3 GB on the disk, one at 13 GB, one at 29 GB, and one after deleting the extra data again. I filled the disk with random data so nothing could compress it. Then there was one snapshot with the Droplet powered off, for comparison.

The Droplet didn't notice

I half expected writes to slow down while the snapshot was being taken. They didn't. During the 13 to 184 seconds each snapshot took, the 99th percentile of Postgres commit times stayed between 2.8 and 5.7 ms, no higher than the 5.5 to 6.5 ms of the rest of the run. The longest gap between two consecutive writes during any snapshot was 38 ms, and outside the snapshots it went up to 42 ms.

So on this Droplet, at this write rate, the "performance degradation" the docs mention didn't show up at all.

The disk is frozen three seconds after you ask

Every live snapshot captured the disk at a single moment, between 3.0 and 3.25 seconds after I sent the request. I can see that moment precisely because both writers stamp their lines with the time: in the restored copy, the last row in Postgres and the last line in the fsynced file were always within 7 milliseconds of each other. Everything written after that moment was missing, and nothing written before it was.

That makes a live snapshot the same as pulling the power cable at that instant. Which is a case Postgres is built for.

Postgres was fine every time

Every restored copy came up with Postgres saying "database system was not properly shut down; automatic recovery in progress". It replayed its write-ahead log for 0.13 to 0.64 seconds and started. The table was complete in all six: no gaps in the numbering, every row up to the moment of the freeze, nothing half-written. The fsynced file was the same. Not one torn or damaged line in six snapshots.

So the docs' warning about databases is worth taking seriously, but for Postgres with its default fsync and full_page_writes on, a live snapshot is a crash it knows how to recover from. A database or an app that doesn't flush its writes is a different story, which the other file showed.

The file without fsync was up to 26 seconds behind

The file that was never fsynced was behind in every live snapshot, by between 0.7 and 26.4 seconds. And it didn't just stop early. Each one ended with a run of zero bytes, between 704 and 3,392 of them, where lines should have been. The file's size had already been saved, always on a 4 KB boundary, but the last stretch of its contents hadn't reached the disk.

The 26 seconds made sense once I looked at how the disk is mounted. DigitalOcean's Ubuntu image mounts the root filesystem with commit=30, so ext4 only commits its journal every 30 seconds, instead of the usual 5. Data that's only in the page cache can be up to 30 seconds old at the moment the snapshot freezes it.

If your app writes logs, uploads or a queue to plain files without fsyncing them, a live snapshot can lose the last half minute of them, and leave zeros behind instead of a clean cut.

Powering off first

With the Droplet shut down through the API, the snapshot had nothing to catch in flight. The restored copy had every row and every line in both files, and Postgres started without any recovery.

The cost is downtime. From the shutdown request until I could SSH back in was 66 seconds: 8 to shut down, 32 for the snapshot, and 26 for the power-on action and the boot. A 2.3 GB snapshot taken live took 13 to 35 seconds, and the Droplet kept serving the whole time.

Bigger disks take longer, both ways

Data on disk Snapshot size Snapshot took Restored Droplet active after
2.3 GB 2.27–2.33 GB 13–35 s 34–37 s
13 GB 13.04 GB 147 s 95 s
29 GB 29.16 GB 184 s 114 s

The snapshot size followed the data on the disk, not the 50 GB size of the disk. The time to take it grew, but not in step with the size: 13 times the data took about 5 to 14 times as long. Restoring grew too. A Droplet created from the 29 GB snapshot took 114 seconds to become active, three times as long as one from the small snapshot, plus another 10 to 20 seconds before SSH answered.

Since DigitalOcean charges $0.06 per GB a month for snapshots, based on the size of the snapshot, that 29 GB one would have cost about $1.75 a month to keep.

Deleting data shrinks the next snapshot

After the 29 GB snapshot I deleted the random files and took another one. It was 2.33 GB. I'd expected it to stay big until I ran fstrim, since deleting a file only marks its blocks free in the filesystem. But the same mount options include discard, so ext4 tells the disk about freed blocks straight away. Running fstrim afterwards reported 21.1 GiB trimmed, and the snapshot after that was still 2.33 GB.

What I got wrong

I thought the snapshot would have to include the deleted data, and planned the fstrim step to show how much it would save. It saved nothing, because the image already discards on delete. I should have looked at the mount options before designing that part.

I also tried to measure the clock difference between my laptop and the Droplet over SSH, so I could line the freeze moment up with the API's timeline. Each round trip took half a second, mostly connection setup, so the result was useless. I measured everything against the request time recorded on my side and the timestamps written on the Droplet instead, and both clocks were synced over NTP.

And my first comparison of write latency "during" and "outside" the snapshot showed a 46-second gap outside it. That was my script measuring straight across the window it was supposed to leave out. The real longest gap was 42 ms.

Caveats

This is one Droplet size, one region, one write rate, and Postgres with default settings. Each size was snapshotted once, and the timings at the small size varied from 13 to 35 seconds, so the bigger ones could vary as much. I didn't test Volumes, which aren't part of a Droplet snapshot, or databases other than Postgres.

The whole run, eight snapshots and seven restored Droplets over about 35 minutes, cost less than five cents.

What I'd take from it

  • A live snapshot is a power cut at one moment, about three seconds after you ask. Anything that survives a power cut survives it.
  • Postgres with default settings recovered in under a second every time, with nothing missing.
  • Anything you write without fsync can be up to 30 seconds behind on these images, and the file may end in zeros. Stop those writers, or power off, if those files matter.
  • Powering off gives you a clean copy for about a minute of downtime on a small Droplet.
  • The snapshot is the size of your data, and deleted data really is gone from it on DigitalOcean's Ubuntu image.

title: Trivy Setup Guide: Installing the Ultimate Open-Source Security Scanner
summary:
Catching weak spots in your software early is far easier than dealing with breaches after deployment. Trivy, a free and fast vulnerability scanner created by Aqua Security, scans container images (like Docker), file systems, and code repositories against global security databases all without complex rules or heavy database setups.

In this quick guide, I cover everything needed to get Trivy running on Ubuntu and Debian systems:

System Prerequisites: Preparing your Linux environment with the essential tools and permissions.

Key & Repository Setup: Adding Aqua Security’s official security key and package source so you can download verified software safely.

Installation & Verification: Installing Trivy via your package manager and confirming it is ready to scan your projects.

title: TermSSH: SSH, Files, Monitoring, and Databases in One Browser Workspace
summary:
TermSSH: SSH, Files, Monitoring, and Databases in One Browser Workspace

If you manage remote servers, your workflow probably looks something like this:

  1. Open an SSH session.
  2. Check the application service.
  3. Read the logs.
  4. Edit a configuration file.
  5. Inspect resource usage.
  6. Open a database client.
  7. Repeat on staging.

TermSSH brings these tasks into a shared browser workspace, using the SSH access you already have.

The website calls the application Secure Console, and its public walkthrough covers much more than an embedded terminal.

What’s inside?

Area Advertised capabilities
SSH terminal Full browser shell, keyboard and colour support, sessions that continue across pages, automatic reconnection
Server connections Saved servers and trusted host-key checking before credentials are sent
Remote files Drag-and-drop uploads and in-place configuration editing
Monitoring Live CPU, memory, disk, and network information
Databases PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, and SQLite
Database operations Browse and edit data, run SQL, import/export dumps, copy databases, and manage users
Automation Saved commands and deployment scripts across one or multiple servers, with retained output
Alerts Telegram and email notifications
Sign-in Email, GitHub, and Google options

Why the SSH-based approach matters

The product describes working without installing an extra agent on your managed servers or opening an additional server port.

For an existing environment, that is a practical design choice: build on the remote access you already maintain.

The database workflow follows the same idea. TermSSH advertises database access through its SSH-based workflow without requiring an additional database port to be opened.

  • Select the saved server.
  • Open the terminal and inspect the service.
  • Check CPU and memory usage.
  • Review or edit a remote configuration file.
  • Run a SQL query to investigate application data.
  • Use a saved deployment script for the next rollout.

Those are separate jobs, but they belong to the same investigation. Keeping them in one workspace can make the process easier to follow.

The published security policy documents encrypted credential storage using AES-256-GCM, TLS/WSS transport, and TOTP MFA support.

title: Fix OOM Kills and MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED on ClickHouse® Servers
summary:
Introduction

ClickHouse® servers can experience two types of memory-related failures.

In the first, the Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminates clickhouse-server. The service restarts, and all running queries fail.

In the second, multiple queries fail with MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (code 241). The error message contains (total), indicating that the entire server has reached its memory limit rather than an individual query exceeding its own limit.

Both failures have the same underlying cause: the server is attempting to use more memory than the host can provide.

In this guide, we'll explain how ClickHouse manages server memory, how to identify the source of memory failures, and how to configure appropriate limits to protect your server.

1. Why Memory Failures Happen

ClickHouse maintains a hard memory limit for the entire server. When a query attempts an allocation that would exceed this limit, the query is stopped.

Two steps determine the server's memory limit.

Step 1: Establishing the Memory Ceiling

At startup, ClickHouse calculates its memory ceiling using the available memory and the setting max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio.

The default value is 0.9, meaning ClickHouse can use up to 90% of the available memory for its server memory limit.

The setting max_server_memory_usage defaults to 0, which means no fixed limit is configured. If you specify a fixed value, ClickHouse uses the lower of that value and the calculated ceiling.

For example, on a host with 13.55 GiB of RAM, setting a fixed limit of 15.63 GiB resulted in the following log message:

Lowered setting 'max_server_memory_usage' to 12.20 GiB because the system has too little memory. The new value was calculated as 13.55 GiB available memory * 0.90 max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio

ClickHouse automatically lowered the configured limit because the host could not support the requested amount.

Step 2: Understanding the Runtime Memory Limit

ClickHouse also uses a background thread called the memory worker to recalculate the hard memory limit while the server is running.

The runtime limit is calculated using:

(resident memory + available system memory) * ratio

The result cannot exceed the previously established ceiling.

When other processes consume memory, the available system memory decreases, and the runtime limit can fall accordingly.

For example:

MemoryWorker: Adjusting total memory hard limit from 5.62 GiB to 5.69 GiB (resident: 364.99 MiB, available: 5.97 GiB, ceiling: 12.20 GiB, ratio: 0.9)

The calculation is approximately:

(0.36 GiB + 5.97 GiB) × 0.9 = 5.69 GiB

Although the ceiling remained at 12.20 GiB, the live limit stayed around 6 GiB because other processes were consuming some of the host's memory.

Why the Safety Margin Matters

The ratio provides a safety margin because ClickHouse's memory tracker does not account for every memory allocation.

In one test, MemoryResident was 940 MiB while TrackedMemory was only 365 MiB. The remaining memory was consumed by the kernel, other services, and allocator overhead.

A sudden memory spike can consume the available margin between memory-worker checks, potentially triggering the Linux OOM killer.

What Happens in Containers?

ClickHouse can read memory limits imposed through cgroups.

For example, after setting MemoryMax=8G with systemd and restarting the server, the log showed:

Changed setting 'max_server_memory_usage' to 7.20 GiB (8.00 GiB available memory * 0.90 max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio)

Without a container memory limit, ClickHouse may see the memory available on the entire host rather than the amount intended for the service.

The setting memory_worker_use_cgroup controls the use of cgroup memory information for runtime memory-limit calculations. However, a test on a host with similar free memory inside and outside the limit does not, by itself, prove the behavior.

Version note: In ClickHouse 26.3.9, memory_worker_dynamic_hard_limit does not exist. The limit remains at the ceiling, making the memory ratio an important protection mechanism.

2. How to Confirm the Problem

Before changing settings, determine whether the operating system killed the process or ClickHouse stopped a query because of its own memory limit.

Step 1: Check for OOM Kills

Run:

sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E "out of memory|killed process"

You can also inspect kernel logs from the last 24 hours:

sudo journalctl -k --since "24 hours ago" | grep -i -E "out of memory|killed process"

Check when the ClickHouse service last started:

systemctl show clickhouse-server -p ActiveEnterTimestamp

If the service started recently and the kernel logs show that clickhouse-serv was killed, the operating system likely terminated the process due to memory pressure.

The kernel truncates process names to 15 characters, which explains why the process name may appear as clickhouse-serv.

Step 2: Find Server-Level Memory Errors

A ClickHouse server-level memory failure typically appears as MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED with error code 241 and (total) in the message.

For example, this error was observed on ClickHouse 26.8.36:

Code: 241. DB::Exception: (total) memory limit exceeded: would use 6.28 GiB (attempt to allocate chunk of 4.00 GiB), current RSS: 2.23 GiB, maximum: 6.08 GiB. OvercommitTracker decision: Query was selected to stop by OvercommitTracker. Untracked memory across all threads: -6.82 MiB: While executing AggregatingTransform. (MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED)

The maximum value represents the live server memory limit. It may be lower than the configured ceiling.

To find recent server-level memory errors, query system.query_log:

SELECT
    event_time,
    query_id,
    substring(exception, 1, 250) AS exception_start
FROM system.query_log
WHERE type = 'ExceptionWhileProcessing'
  AND exception_code = 241
  AND exception LIKE '%(total)%'
  AND event_time > now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
ORDER BY event_time DESC
LIMIT 20;

The system.errors table contains error counts accumulated since the server started and is reset on restart. The query log provides historical records of individual failures.

Step 3: Compare Process Memory with Host Memory

Run the following query:

SELECT
    metric,
    formatReadableSize(value) AS size
FROM system.asynchronous_metrics
WHERE metric IN (
    'MemoryResident',
    'TrackedMemory',
    'OSMemoryTotal',
    'OSMemoryAvailable'
)
ORDER BY metric;

These metrics help you compare the memory used by ClickHouse with the total and available memory on the host.

Step 4: Read the Live Memory Limit

Use system.server_settings to inspect the current server memory limit:

SELECT
    formatReadableSize(toUInt64(value)) AS live_limit
FROM system.server_settings
WHERE name = 'max_server_memory_usage';

This shows the effective limit, which may differ from the value in your configuration file.

For more information about runtime adjustments, inspect the server logs:

sudo grep -a "Adjusting total memory hard limit" /var/log/clickhouse-server/clickhouse-server.log | tail -5

These messages are available at Trace log level.

3. Understanding the Relevant Settings

The following defaults are based on ClickHouse 26.8.36. Verify them on your own server before making changes.

Run:

SELECT
    name,
    value,
    default,
    changed,
    changeable_without_restart
FROM system.server_settings
WHERE name LIKE 'max_server_memory%'
   OR name LIKE 'memory_worker%';

The important settings are:

Setting Default Purpose Restart required
max_server_memory_usage 0 Defines a fixed server memory limit in bytes. A higher value is lowered to the calculated ceiling. No
max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio 0.9 Controls the share of memory available to the server and determines the memory ceiling. A value of 0 disables the limits established by this ratio. No in the test described
memory_worker_dynamic_hard_limit true Allows the memory worker to recalculate the hard limit at runtime. Yes
memory_worker_use_cgroup true Uses cgroup memory information when calculating the runtime limit. Yes

The changeable_without_restart column may show No for the ratio setting. In the test described here, reloading the configuration still applied the change, and the logs showed a new Changed setting message.

If the expected log message does not appear after reloading the configuration, restart the server.

4. How to Fix Memory Failures

The recommended approach is to reserve memory for the operating system and configure explicit memory limits for containers.

Step 1: Set a Lower Memory Ratio

Create a configuration file at:

/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/memory.xml

Add the following configuration:


    0.8

A ratio of 0.8 allows ClickHouse to use up to 80% of the available memory for its server memory limit.

For example, on a host with 64 GiB of memory, the ceiling would be 51.2 GiB, leaving 12.8 GiB for the operating system and other processes.

Consider these starting points:

  • 0.8: A reasonable starting point for many hosts.
  • 0.7: Consider this when the host runs other services.
  • 0.85: Consider this only on a dedicated host with carefully monitored memory usage.

These values are starting points, not universal recommendations. The appropriate ratio depends on the host, workload, and memory consumed by other processes.

Reload the configuration:

SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG;

Then verify the updated setting in the logs:

sudo grep -a "max_server_memory_usage" /var/log/clickhouse-server/clickhouse-server.log | tail -3

You should see a Changed setting message confirming the new value.

For example, a test using a ratio of 0.15 produced:

Changed setting 'max_server_memory_usage' to 2.03 GiB (13.55 GiB available memory * 0.15 max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio)

Configuration tip: Write the new file in a separate directory first, then copy it into config.d/. This reduces the chance of ClickHouse loading a partially written configuration file.

Step 2: Configure a Fixed Memory Limit

If you know how much memory ClickHouse should use on a shared host, you can set an explicit limit alongside the ratio.

Update memory.xml:


    0.8
    53687091200

The value 53687091200 represents 50 GiB in bytes.

A fixed limit makes the memory budget easier to understand and manage. ClickHouse uses the lowest applicable value among the fixed limit, the calculated ceiling, and the runtime limit.

Reload the configuration:

SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG;

In the test described here, changing the configured value from 3 GiB to 2 GiB through a configuration reload caused the next memory error to report:

maximum: 2.00 GiB

Verify the effective limit in the logs and through system.server_settings.

Step 3: Set a Container Memory Limit

A container memory limit prevents ClickHouse from consuming the entire host's memory.

Docker example:

docker run -d --name clickhouse --memory=32g clickhouse/clickhouse-server

Kubernetes example:

resources:
  requests:
    memory: 32Gi
  limits:
    memory: 32Gi

Setting the Kubernetes memory request equal to the limit reserves the same memory amount for scheduling purposes and helps avoid unexpected memory-pressure evictions caused by overcommitting the requested amount.

With a 32 GiB container limit and a ratio of 0.8, the calculated ceiling is 25.6 GiB.

Systemd's MemoryMax provides a similar cgroup memory limit.

Remember that the container limit and ClickHouse's internal memory limit serve different purposes: the container constrains the process at the operating-system level, while ClickHouse's settings help it stop queries before reaching that boundary.

5. How to Verify the Fix

After changing the configuration, check the effective settings and confirm that the logs show the expected memory limit.

On a test server, you can trigger a memory-limit error using:

SELECT groupArray(number)
FROM numbers(100000000000)
SETTINGS max_memory_usage = 0
FORMAT Null;

Warning: Do not run this test on a production server. It is intended for controlled testing only.

The query should fail with code 241. The maximum value in the error should match the configured effective limit or be lower if the host has insufficient available memory.

For production, monitor the server for seven days after applying the changes.

The fix is working as intended when:

  1. Kernel logs show no new OOM kills.
  2. The query log contains no new unexpected (total) memory-limit errors.
  3. MemoryResident remains below OSMemoryTotal with a safe memory margin.

Continue monitoring workloads that generate large aggregations, memory-intensive queries, merges, and mutations.

6. Risks and Trade-Offs

Lower Limits Can Cause Queries to Fail Earlier

Reducing the memory limit means ClickHouse may reject queries that previously succeeded.

This is often the correct trade-off: a failed query is preferable to a server process being killed and disrupting all running queries.

Identify and tune the heaviest queries rather than simply increasing the server limit.

The Live Limit Can Change

On a shared host, the effective memory limit can decrease when other processes consume more memory.

As a result, queries may fail even when the configured settings have not changed. Investigate other processes and host-level memory usage before increasing ClickHouse's limits.

Merges and Mutations Have Their Own Memory Controls

Merges and mutations have a separate setting:

merges_mutations_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio

Its default is 0.5. Review it when diagnosing memory pressure related to background operations.

Caches Also Consume Memory

Caches contribute to memory consumption. Avoid increasing cache sizes when lowering the server's memory limit unless you have measured the impact and confirmed that sufficient memory remains available.

Be Careful When Using Swap

The setting description notes that low-RAM hosts with swap may require a ratio above 1 in certain situations.

This should only be done deliberately. Allowing ClickHouse to use swap before reaching its configured limit may delay an OOM event, but heavy swapping can make queries extremely slow and postpone rather than prevent a more severe failure.

For ClickHouse hosts, consider disabling swap or configuring a low vm.swappiness value according to your operational requirements.

7. Summary

When troubleshooting ClickHouse memory failures:

  • Check dmesg and the service start time to determine whether the operating system killed the process.
  • Look for MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED code 241 errors containing (total) to identify server-level memory failures.
  • Read the maximum value in the error message to understand the effective live limit.
  • Remember that the live limit is constrained by the fixed limit, the ratio-based ceiling, and the runtime limit calculated by the memory worker.
  • Configure a suitable max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio in config.d/ and reload the configuration.
  • Set an explicit container memory limit when running ClickHouse in Docker, Kubernetes, or another cgroup-managed environment.
  • Monitor kernel logs, query errors, and memory metrics after applying the fix.

The goal is not to let ClickHouse consume every available byte of memory. It is to establish a predictable memory budget that protects the server while allowing normal workloads to run reliably.

  • ClickHouse documentation: max_server_memory_usage and max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio.

Reducing the memory limit means ClickHouse may reject queries that previously succeeded.

This is often the correct trade-off: a failed query is preferable to a server process being killed and disrupting all running queries.

title: GitHub Actions Self-Hosted Runners Documentation (2026): Requirements, macOS, Online Status and Warm Pools
summary:

This reference collects those facts with the exact commands, then shows how to keep a runner online, how to cut self-hosted runner startup time with a warm pool, and when a hosted Linux runner at $0.001 a minute replaces the fleet entirely.

Where the GitHub Actions self-hosted runners documentation lives

These are the GitHub Docs pages an engineer needs, by topic:

  • Self-hosted runners (concepts): what a self-hosted runner is, and the repository, organization and enterprise levels.
  • Self-hosted runners reference: machine requirements, supported operating systems and architectures, routing precedence, autoscaling, runner software updates and network communication.
  • Adding self-hosted runners: the registration steps with config.sh.
  • Configuring the self-hosted runner application as a service: svc.sh, the way to keep a runner online after a reboot.

  • Actions Runner Controller: the Kubernetes autoscaling reference implementation, also documented in the actions/actions-runner-controller repository on GitHub.

Key numbers from the self-hosted runner docs

Rule Value GitHub Docs page

Minimum network speed, upload and download 70 kilobits per second Self-hosted runners reference

Minimum macOS version macOS 11.0 (Big Sur) Self-hosted runners reference

Self-hosted runner requirements: operating systems and architectures

The Self-hosted runners reference lists three requirements for a runner machine: it can install and run the runner application, it can communicate with GitHub Actions, and it has enough hardware for your workflows. The runner application itself uses minimal resources.

  • Windows: Windows 10 64-bit, Windows 11 64-bit, Windows Server 2016, 2019 and 2022 64-bit.
  • macOS: macOS 11.0 (Big Sur) or later.

Supported processor architectures: x64 on Linux, macOS and Windows, and ARM64 on Linux, macOS and Windows, a line the page marks as public preview.

One rule catches many teams: Docker container actions and service containers require a Linux runner with Docker installed.

macOS runners cannot run Docker container actions or service containers, since those require Linux. A common split is macOS for iOS and Xcode builds and Linux for everything else, and the Linux side is where the bulk of CI minutes go.

Add a self-hosted runner: exact steps

  1. Open the repository, organization or enterprise settings, then Actions, Runners, New self-hosted runner.
  2. Pick the OS and architecture, and run the download commands GitHub shows.
  3. Register the runner with the scope URL and registration token from that page. Here RUNNER_SCOPE_URL is your repository or organization URL on GitHub, exactly as the New self-hosted runner page prints it:

  1. Start it in the foreground to test:

  1. Target it from a workflow by labels, or by runner group plus labels: 
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on:
      group: build-runners
      labels: [self-hosted, linux, x64]

The Self-hosted runners concepts page explains scope: repository-level runners serve one repository, organization-level runners serve many repositories, and enterprise-level runners can be assigned to multiple organizations.

Runner online status: "runner must be online" and "job queued until runner online"

The routing precedence section of the Self-hosted runners reference defines availability exactly:

  • If GitHub finds an online and idle runner matching the job's runs-on labels and groups, it assigns the job to that runner.
  • If that runner does not pick up the job within 60 seconds, the job is re-queued for another runner.
  • If no online and idle runner matches, the job remains queued until a runner comes online.
  • If the job stays queued for more than 24 hours, it fails.

A labeled job with no matching runner does not fail at queue time; it waits out the 24-hour window. Offline means the runner application is not running or cannot reach GitHub.

# Linux (systemd)

sudo ./svc.sh start
sudo ./svc.sh status

On macOS, run the same commands without sudo. On Windows, the config.cmd registration prompt offers to run the runner as a service.

Three things keep a persistent runner Idle instead of Offline:

  2. Outbound HTTPS on port 443 stays open to the GitHub domains listed in the reference (see the communication section below).
  3. The runner version stays current. If a runner is not updated within 63 days of a new version, GitHub stops assigning jobs to it.

  • GitHub Actions Runner Scale Set Client: an open source Go module (the actions/scaleset repository) for building autoscaling on VMs, containers or on-premises hardware outside Kubernetes.

From the communication section of the Self-hosted runners reference: the host needs at least 70 kilobits per second up and down and outbound HTTPS on port 443. The page groups the required GitHub domains by function: essential operations, downloading actions, uploading and downloading logs, artifacts, job summaries and caches, runner version updates, OIDC tokens, GitHub Packages and containers, Git Large File Storage, Dependabot jobs and release assets. title: 33 Most Used Linux Commands
summary:
Recently, when I decided to transition my career from Data analytics to Cloud & Devops engineer, and I discovered that learning linux was non-negotiable if I wanted a smoother journey.

Naturally, I started asking around to see if learning linux was difficult as people made it out to be. The consensus ? " linux is not inherently hard", instead it is being split into two distinct experiences, graphical user interface and command line interface.

Depending on your goals, it can be incredibly simple or deeply technical

But what exactly is the difference, and which one is the most critical for a DevOps Engineer to master?

Graphical User Interface (GUI) allows you to interact with a system using visual elements like icons, windows, and mouse clicks, the Command Line Interface (CLI) relies entirely on typing text-based commands into a terminal.

The core goal of DevOps is automation, scale, and speed. The GUI fundamentally breaks this goal, while the CLI enables it.

This blog post mainly showcase 33 important CLI commands every Cloud & Devops engineer should know if they want a smoother jounery.

📂 1. File & Directory Navigation

Before you can automate infrastructure, you have to know how to move around it.
• pwd (Print Working Directory): Shows you exactly where you are in the file system.
• ls (List): Lists all files and folders in your current directory. Use ls -la to show hidden file (files starting with dot) in additional to normal file. Use ls -lh to show file size in KB, MB or GB instaed of raw byte.
• cd (Change Directory): Moves you between folders (e.g., cd /var/log). Use cd ~ to teleport back to user's home directory. Use cd .. to move from current location to parent directory. Use cd - to swap back to the directory you were in before this one.
• mkdir (Make Directory): Creates a new folder (e.g., mkdir my-app).
• rmdir (Remove Directory): Deletes an empty directory.

📝 2. File Manipulation & Viewing

As a DevOps engineer, you will constantly edit configuration files, read logs, and move scripts around.
• touch: Creates a blank file instantly (e.g., touch deployment.yaml).
• cp (Copy): Copies files or directories. Use cp -r to copy folders recursively.
• mv (Move): Moves or renames files and directories.
• rm (Remove): Deletes files. Use rm -rf with caution to delete folders and their contents forcefully.
• cat (Concatenate): Displays the entire contents of a file on your screen.
• head / tail: Shows the beginning or end of a file. tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log is essential for watching live logs.
• nano / vim: Text editors built directly into the terminal for modifying scripts and configurations.

🛡️ 3. Permissions & User Management

Linux handles security strictly. You must understand ownership to deploy applications safely.
• chmod (Change Mode): Alters file and folder permissions (e.g., chmod +x script.sh makes a script executable).
• chown (Change Owner): Changes the user and/or group ownership of a file.
• sudo (Superuser Do): Runs a command with administrative/root privileges.
• whoami: Displays the username of the current active session.

🔍 4. Searching & Text Processing

Infrastructure generates massive logs. These commands help you find exactly what you are looking for in seconds.
• grep: Searches for specific text patterns inside files (e.g., grep "ERROR" app.log).
• find: Searches for files and directories based on names, sizes, or dates.
• awk / sed: Powerful text processing tools used to manipulate and filter data streams inside automation scripts.

⚙️ 5. System Monitoring & Process Management

Cloud instances can run out of memory or freeze. You need to know how to check system health.
• top / htop: Displays interactive, real-time views of system resources, CPU, and RAM usage.
• ps (Process Status): Lists currently running processes. Often paired with grep (e.g., ps aux | grep node).
• kill: Stops a running process using its Process ID (PID).
• df (Disk Free): Shows available and used disk space across your system file paths.
• free: Displays total, used, and available physical and swap memory (RAM).

🌐 6. Networking & Connectivity

DevOps is entirely about connecting systems. These commands debug network traffic and APIs.
• ping: Tests the network connectivity between your machine and a remote host.
• curl / wget: Tools to download files or make HTTP requests to test APIs and web servers directly from the CLI.
• netstat / ss: Checks active network connections and identifies which applications are listening on specific ports.
• ip addr: Displays IP addresses and network interface details for your machine.
• ssh (Secure Shell): Logs you into remote Linux cloud servers securely over an encrypted connection.

Practice them all in a local machine. Mastering these commands is your first major step toward dominating terminal, and you'll find your transition into Cloud and DevOps or any related field seamless.

Graphical User Interface (GUI) allows you to interact with a system using visual elements like icons, windows, and mouse clicks, the Command Line Interface (CLI) relies entirely on typing text-based commands into a terminal.

The core goal of DevOps is automation, scale, and speed. The GUI fundamentally breaks this goal, while the CLI enables it.

This blog post mainly showcase 33 important CLI commands every Cloud & Devops engineer should know if they want a smoother jounery.

📂 1. File & Directory Navigation

Before you can automate infrastructure, you have to know how to move around it.
• pwd (Print Working Directory): Shows you exactly where you are in the file system.
• ls (List): Lists all files and folders in your current directory. Use ls -la to show hidden file (files starting with dot) in additional to normal file. Use ls -lh to show file size in KB, MB or GB instaed of raw byte.
• cd (Change Directory): Moves you between folders (e.g., cd /var/log). Use cd ~ to teleport back to user's home directory. Use cd .. to move from current location to parent directory. Use cd - to swap back to the directory you were in before this one.
• mkdir (Make Directory): Creates a new folder (e.g., mkdir my-app).
• rmdir (Remove Directory): Deletes an empty directory.

📝 2. File Manipulation & Viewing

As a DevOps engineer, you will constantly edit configuration files, read logs, and move scripts around.
• touch: Creates a blank file instantly (e.g., touch deployment.yaml).
• cp (Copy): Copies files or directories. Use cp -r to copy folders recursively.
• mv (Move): Moves or renames files and directories.
• rm (Remove): Deletes files. Use rm -rf with caution to delete folders and their contents forcefully.
• cat (Concatenate): Displays the entire contents of a file on your screen.
• head / tail: Shows the beginning or end of a file. tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log is essential for watching live logs.
• nano / vim: Text editors built directly into the terminal for modifying scripts and configurations.

🛡️ 3. Permissions & User Management

Linux handles security strictly. You must understand ownership to deploy applications safely.
• chmod (Change Mode): Alters file and folder permissions (e.g., chmod +x script.sh makes a script executable).
• chown (Change Owner): Changes the user and/or group ownership of a file.
• sudo (Superuser Do): Runs a command with administrative/root privileges.
• whoami: Displays the username of the current active session.

🔍 4. Searching & Text Processing

Infrastructure generates massive logs. These commands help you find exactly what you are looking for in seconds.
• grep: Searches for specific text patterns inside files (e.g., grep "ERROR" app.log).
• find: Searches for files and directories based on names, sizes, or dates.
• awk / sed: Powerful text processing tools used to manipulate and filter data streams inside automation scripts.

⚙️ 5. System Monitoring & Process Management

Cloud instances can run out of memory or freeze. You need to know how to check system health.
• top / htop: Displays interactive, real-time views of system resources, CPU, and RAM usage.
• ps (Process Status): Lists currently running processes. Often paired with grep (e.g., ps aux | grep node).
• kill: Stops a running process using its Process ID (PID).
• df (Disk Free): Shows available and used disk space across your system file paths.
• free: Displays total, used, and available physical and swap memory (RAM).

🌐 6. Networking & Connectivity

DevOps is entirely about connecting systems. These commands debug network traffic and APIs.
• ping: Tests the network connectivity between your machine and a remote host.
• curl / wget: Tools to download files or make HTTP requests to test APIs and web servers directly from the CLI.
• netstat / ss: Checks active network connections and identifies which applications are listening on specific ports.
• ip addr: Displays IP addresses and network interface details for your machine.
• ssh (Secure Shell): Logs you into remote Linux cloud servers securely over an encrypted connection.

Practice them all in a local machine. Mastering these commands is your first major step toward dominating terminal, and you'll find your transition into Cloud and DevOps or any related field seamless.

title: Setting Up LVM Storage for Orthanc PACS & MySQL: Combining Remaining OS Disk Space with Dedicated Storage
summary:
Dalam mengelola server Orthanc PACS di lingkungan rumah sakit atau klinik, pertumbuhan data DICOM (CT-Scan, MRI, X-Ray) terjadi sangat cepat. Mengandalkan partisi statis biasa akan menyulitkan ekspansi kapasitas di masa depan karena berisiko membutuhkan downtime atau migrasi ulang jutaan file.

Solusi terbaik di tingkat sistem operasi adalah menggabungkan Hardware RAID (untuk proteksi kegagalan fisik) dengan LVM (Logical Volume Manager) di Linux. Dengan arsitektur ini, kapasitas dari beberapa Virtual Disk dapat digabung menjadi satu pool besar, dipisah antara database dan file DICOM, serta dapat diperbesar secara online kapan saja.

Arsitektur Storage

Pada skenario ini, sistem memiliki dua block device hasil konfigurasi Hardware RAID. Pada fisiknya memiliki 1862.5 GB x 4 Slot (vd_os) dan 3725.5 GB x 2 slot (vd_data)

  1. /dev/sdb (~3.6 TB): Disk utama yang sudah terinstal sistem operasi secara non-LVM (sdb1 /boot/efi, sdb2 /, sdb3 swap) dan masih memiliki ruang kosong sekitar 3.5 TB.
  2. /dev/sda (~3.6 TB): Virtual Disk kedua yang masih kosong utuh.

Kedua sumber ruang tersebut digabung ke dalam satu Volume Group (vg_orthanc), lalu dipecah menjadi dua Logical Volume (LV) terpisah:

  • lv_mysql_orthanc (100 GB): Khusus untuk direktori data database MySQL/Percona (indeks PACS).
  • lv_orthanc (~6.94 TB): Khusus untuk penyimpanan fisik file .dcm Orthanc (mengambil 98% dari sisa ruang bebas dan menyisakan 2% cadangan di Volume Group).

Mengapa database dan storage DICOM dipisah LV-nya?
Jika suatu saat penyimpanan file DICOM penuh hingga 100%, database MySQL tidak akan ikut macet atau corrupt karena gagal menulis transaction log. Selain itu, backup atau LVM snapshot database bisa dilakukan secara independen.

1. Membuat Partisi Sisa pada Disk OS (/dev/sdb4)

Langkah pertama adalah mengalokasikan ruang kosong di ujung /dev/sdb menjadi partisi ke-4 dengan flag LVM. Pastikan titik awal (start) sesuai dengan titik akhir partisi ke-3 (111GB pada output parted /dev/sdb unit GB print):

parted -a optimal /dev/sdb mkpart primary 111GB 100%
parted /dev/sdb set 4 lvm on
partprobe /dev/sdb

Verifikasi:

parted /dev/sdb unit GB print

Pastikan baris nomor 4 muncul mulai dari 111GB hingga 4000GB dengan flag lvm.

2. Membuat Physical Volume (PV) & Volume Group (vg_orthanc)

Inisialisasi partisi sisa disk OS (/dev/sdb4) dan seluruh disk kosong (/dev/sda tanpa perlu dipartisi) menjadi Physical Volume, lalu satukan ke dalam Volume Group vg_orthanc:

pvcreate /dev/sdb4 /dev/sda
vgcreate vg_orthanc /dev/sdb4 /dev/sda

Verifikasi:

vgs

Pastikan vg_orthanc terdaftar dengan PV = 2 dan total VSize sekitar 7.17t.

3. Membagi Menjadi 2 Logical Volume (Database & DICOM)

Buat dua Logical Volume secara terpisah di dalam vg_orthanc:

# 1. LV Database MySQL/Percona (100 GB)
lvcreate -L 100G -n lv_mysql_orthanc vg_orthanc

# 2. LV Storage DICOM Orthanc (98% dari sisa ruang bebas)
lvcreate -l 98%FREE -n lv_orthanc vg_orthanc

Verifikasi:

lvs

Pastikan lv_mysql_orthanc (100.00g) dan lv_orthanc (<6.94t) berstatus aktif (-wi-a-----).

4. Mengecek Sisa Cadangan 2% di Volume Group

Penggunaan 98%FREE menyisakan sekitar 2% ruang bebas (free extents) di dalam Volume Group. Cadangan ini berfungsi untuk membuat LVM snapshot darurat atau memperbesar ukuran lv_mysql_orthanc sewaktu-waktu tanpa perlu mengecilkan partisi DICOM.

Untuk melihat secara pasti berapa GB sisa ruang tersebut:

vgs --units g

Atau untuk tampilan detail PE (Physical Extents):

vgdisplay vg_orthanc | grep -E "VG Size|Alloc PE|Free  PE"

Pada kolom VFree (atau baris Free PE / Size), akan terlihat kapasitas cadangan sekitar 144.60g (~144.6 GiB).

5. Format Filesystem XFS & Buat Direktori Mount

Orthanc menyimpan jutaan file DICOM kecil hingga menengah dalam struktur direktori heksadesimal bercabang (00 hingga ff). XFS sangat direkomendasikan dibanding ext4 karena performa penanganan jutaan inode yang jauh lebih cepat serta dukungan ekspansi kapasitas secara online yang stabil. Gunakan jalur /dev//

mkfs.xfs -L mysql_orthanc /dev/vg_orthanc/lv_mysql_orthanc
mkfs.xfs -L orthanc_data /dev/vg_orthanc/lv_orthanc

mkdir -p /mnt/mysql-orthanc
mkdir -p /mnt/orthanc-data

Ambil masing-masing UUID perangkat menggunakan blkid:

blkid /dev/vg_orthanc/*

6. Pasang Permanen di /etc/fstab & Set Permission

Daftarkan kedua UUID ke dalam /etc/fstab dengan opsi noatime (mencegah penulisan timestamp akses setiap kali gambar dibuka) dan logbufs=8 untuk mengoptimalkan performa jurnal XFS:

UUID=   /mnt/mysql-orthanc  xfs  defaults,noatime,logbufs=8  0  2
UUID=         /mnt/orthanc-data   xfs  defaults,noatime,logbufs=8  0  2

Terapkan konfigurasi mount dan atur kepemilikan (ownership) direktori sesuai dengan UID kontainer Docker (UID 999 untuk MySQL/Percona dan UID 1000 untuk osimis/orthanc):

systemctl daemon-reload
mount -a

chown -R 999:999 /mnt/mysql-orthanc
chown -R 1000:1000 /mnt/orthanc-data

Verifikasi Akhir:

df -hT /mnt/mysql-orthanc /mnt/orthanc-data

Pastikan kedua direktori ter-mount sebagai xfs dengan kapasitas 100G dan 7.0T.

Bonus: Ekspansi Kapasitas di Masa Depan (Tanpa Downtime)

Ketika kapasitas penyimpanan DICOM mulai penuh dan Anda menambahkan Virtual Disk baru (misal terbaca sebagai /dev/sdc), perluasan kapasitas dapat dilakukan secara online tanpa mematikan kontainer Orthanc:

pvcreate /dev/sdc
vgextend vg_orthanc /dev/sdc
lvextend -l +98%FREE -r /dev/vg_orthanc/lv_orthanc

Flag -r (--resizefs) akan otomatis menjalankan xfs_growfs secara langsung sehingga kapasitas baru langsung terbaca oleh sistem.

title: The restart budget is a sum, not a default
summary:
Every container runtime has a default grace period between "please stop" and "you are being killed" — ten seconds in Docker's case. It is easy to read that number as a constant of the platform rather than a parameter you chose, and easier still to never measure what your own services do inside it.

Two things follow from treating it as a default instead of a budget.

The sum is what your users experience

If a restart touches six containers that each take the full grace to exit, the unavailable window is not ten seconds; it is up to a minute, plus startup. That total is the number your rollback spends, and it is the one that has to fit inside whatever tolerance the service has.

restart_cost = Σ(stop_grace_period_i + startup_i)   for the containers being replaced

The interesting failure is when the orchestrator's health-check timeout is smaller than that sum. The platform declares the service unhealthy mid-restart, kills it again, and the cycle repeats — a restart loop that looks like a crashing application but is really an arithmetic mismatch between two timeouts set by different people.

The grace period is per service, because drain time is

A queue consumer drains in-flight work; a stateless API does not. Giving them the same number means one of the two is either wasting seconds on every deploy or dying with work in hand. The number worth setting is measured, not inherited: take the 99th percentile of in-flight work duration and add a margin.

The shutdown path is the untested path

Nobody exercises SIGTERM handling in development, because developers kill processes with SIGKILL. So the handler is the least-tested code in the service, and the grace period is where its bugs are billed.

A cheap practice that pays for itself: on every deploy, log the time from signal received to exit. After a few weeks you know each service's real drain time, and the budget above stops being hypothetical.

What to do with it

Add the sum to the deploy budget, next to startup time, and treat it as a cost you pay on every rollback. It is not a large number. It is just a number nobody computes, which is why it shows up as an incident rather than a line item.
